triage.name: Cirrhosis
triage.reason: Rich multisystem diagnosis reachable from history of alcohol or viral hepatitis, exam stigmata, and labs/imaging; classic complications to explore.

review_issues: presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: More common in men, largely reflecting higher rates of alcohol use and viral hepatitis exposure
Higher burden in Black and Hispanic populations in the US, driven by hepatitis C and metabolic liver disease
Increasingly diagnosed in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes due to steatotic liver disease

risk_factors.text: Chronic hepatitis B or hepatitis C infection
Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia)
Injection drug use or other bloodborne exposure
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, or autoimmune hepatitis

family_history: Cirrhosis or liver failure in a first-degree relative
social_history: Injection drug use or shared needles
History of incarceration or blood transfusion before screening
Tattoos or body piercings with unsterile equipment
exposures: Herbal or dietary supplements with hepatotoxic potential

chief_complaints.text: My belly is getting bigger and my legs are swollen
I feel tired all the time
My skin and eyes look yellow
I bruise easily and my gums bleed
I itch all over and can't sleep

hpi.onset: Insidious, developing over months to years; often discovered incidentally on labs or imaging before symptoms appear
hpi.duration: Chronic, typically present for years by the time symptoms bring the patient in
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; symptoms worsen as liver function declines and portal hypertension develops, with episodes of decompensation such as ascites, variceal bleeding, or confusion
hpi.location: Abdomen (fullness, swelling), lower extremities (edema), generalized (fatigue, itching, jaundice)
hpi.quality: Dull abdominal fullness and pressure; aching leg swelling; constant fatigue; generalized itching
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate early, becoming severe with decompensation
hpi.timing: Persistent; abdominal swelling and edema worse later in the day and with salty meals

associated_symptoms.text: Loss of appetite and unintended weight loss
Swelling of the legs and ankles
Decreased sex drive or erectile dysfunction
Fevers or abdominal pain suggesting infection

pertinent_negatives: Severe right upper quadrant pain radiating to the back
Recent travel to an endemic area with acute jaundice
Known cancer diagnosis or weight loss out of proportion to appetite loss

argues_against: Acute infectious hepatitis with high fever

negatives: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back

positives.text: Swelling of the legs and ankles
Shortness of breath when lying flat

argues_against: Congestive heart failure as the primary cause of edema

positives.text: Spider-like blood vessels on the chest and face
Daytime sleepiness or reversed sleep cycle

negatives: Blood clots in the legs or lungs

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, falls, or failure to thrive rather than abdominal swelling or jaundice; symptoms are often attributed to aging.
Can be masked by normal pregnancy changes; may present with severe itching, jaundice, or liver test abnormalities that overlap with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy or HELLP syndrome.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal relationship of symptoms to liver disease
Classic stigmata such as spider angiomata

atypical.how_it_differs: Often asymptomatic and detected on routine labs; may present with unexplained hypoglycemia or worsening glycemic control due to impaired hepatic glucose handling.
Abdominal swelling may be attributed to central adiposity, delaying recognition of ascites; metabolic steatotic liver disease is the likely underlying cause.
missing_classic_features: Visible abdominal distension distinct from fat

atypical.how_it_differs: Already known liver disease may present with decompensation such as encephalopathy, bleeding, or infection rather than new symptoms of cirrhosis itself.

general.mild: Well-appearing or mildly fatigued; may look well despite abnormal labs
general.moderate: Chronically ill-appearing, fatigued, with visible abdominal distension or leg swelling
general.severe: Cachectic and jaundiced, with marked ascites, muscle wasting, and scleral icterus
general.critical: Toxic or encephalopathic, drowsy or confused, with tense ascites, jaundice, and signs of bleeding or infection

findings.maneuver: Inspect the sclerae in natural light
findings.finding: Yellow discoloration of the sclerae (icterus)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the chest, face, and upper trunk
findings.finding: Spider angiomata (central arteriole with radiating vessels that blanch on pressure)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the palms
findings.finding: Diffuse redness of the thenar and hypothenar eminences

findings.maneuver: Inspect the abdominal wall with the patient supine
findings.finding: Dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus (caput medusae)

findings.maneuver: Percuss the flanks and then the midline with the patient supine, then roll the patient to one side
findings.finding: Dullness in the dependent flank that shifts with position (shifting dullness)

findings.maneuver: Place one hand on the midline and tap the opposite flank while an assistant stabilizes the midline
findings.finding: Palpable fluid wave

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant below the costal margin
findings.finding: Enlarged, firm, nodular liver edge

findings.maneuver: Palpate the left upper quadrant and percuss Traube's space
findings.finding: Enlarged spleen

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants
findings.finding: Diffuse abdominal tenderness, which may indicate spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen and observe for involuntary guarding
findings.finding: Involuntary guarding or rigidity suggesting peritonitis

findings.maneuver: Press over the dorsum of the foot and lower shin for several seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the thenar eminence and temporal muscles
findings.finding: Muscle wasting and weakness

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to extend both arms with wrists dorsiflexed and observe for several seconds
findings.finding: Brief, irregular flapping of the hands (asterixis) indicating hepatic encephalopathy

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation, attention, and level of consciousness
findings.finding: Confusion, disorientation, or drowsiness

findings.maneuver: Note the odor of the patient's breath
findings.finding: Sweet, musty breath odor

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the male breast tissue
findings.finding: Breast enlargement

findings.maneuver: Examine the testes
findings.finding: Small, soft testes

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular venous pulsation at 45 degrees
findings.finding: Normal jugular venous pressure without prominent v waves

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all lung fields
findings.finding: Clear breath sounds without crackles or pleural rub

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and palpate the precordium
findings.finding: Normal S1 and S2 without murmur, gallop, or displaced apical impulse

findings.maneuver: Perform a focused neurologic exam including strength and cranial nerves
findings.finding: No focal motor or sensory deficit

labs.caveat: Thrombocytopenia from portal hypertension with splenic sequestration and reduced thrombopoietin; often the earliest lab clue to cirrhosis.
Reflects synthetic failure; a rising INR is a key prognostic marker and part of the MELD score.
Low albumin reflects reduced hepatic synthesis and is a component of the Child-Pugh score; also lowered by inflammation and malnutrition.
Jaundice becomes clinically visible above roughly 2.5–3 mg/dL; a rising level suggests decompensation.
AST is usually greater than ALT in alcohol-related liver disease; aminotransferases may be near normal in advanced cirrhosis because of reduced hepatocyte mass.
Disproportionate elevation suggests a cholestatic process such as primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, or infiltrative disease.
Sensitive but nonspecific marker of hepatobiliary disease and alcohol use.
Dilutional hyponatremia from impaired free-water clearance; a low sodium is a strong prognostic marker and part of MELD-Na.
A normal creatinine can mask significant renal impairment because of reduced muscle mass; hepatorenal syndrome is a feared complication.
Anemia from GI blood loss, hypersplenism, nutritional deficiency, or bone marrow suppression; may be masked by volume overload.
Macrocytosis from alcohol, folate deficiency, or hypersplenism.
Leukopenia from hypersplenism; a rising white count should prompt evaluation for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or other infection.
Poorly correlates with the degree of hepatic encephalopathy; useful mainly when the diagnosis is unclear, not for monitoring.
Hypoglycemia from depleted glycogen stores and impaired gluconeogenesis, especially in acute decompensation.
Negative. Obtained in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or procedures.

findings.finding: Prolonged QT interval
Sinus tachycardia
Nonspecific ST-T flattening or T-wave changes

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging in most patients; no radiation and can assess portal flow

findings.text: Coarse, nodular hepatic echotexture with irregular surface
Splenomegaly
Ascites
Reversed or reduced portal venous flow on Doppler
Recanalized umbilical vein or portosystemic collaterals
Gallstones or gallbladder wall thickening
Focal hepatic lesion requiring further characterization

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected hepatocellular carcinoma, variceal bleeding, or complications such as thrombosis or abscess

findings.text: Nodular liver contour with heterogeneous parenchymal enhancement
Ascites
Splenomegaly and portosystemic varices
Portal or splenic vein thrombosis
Arterial-phase enhancing lesion with washout suggesting hepatocellular carcinoma

imaging.preferred_when: Characterizing focal liver lesions or evaluating the biliary tree when ultrasound and CT are inconclusive

findings.text: Nodular regenerative parenchyma with fibrous septa
Biliary ductal changes suggesting primary sclerosing cholangitis
Focal lesion with characteristic enhancement pattern of hepatocellular carcinoma

imaging.preferred_when: Screening for varices at diagnosis and after acute GI bleeding

findings.text: Esophageal varices, graded by size
Gastric varices or portal hypertensive gastropathy
Actively bleeding varix or stigmata of recent hemorrhage
No varices at screening

imaging.preferred_when: Estimating fibrosis noninvasively when the diagnosis is uncertain

findings.text: Markedly elevated liver stiffness consistent with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis
Elevated hemidiaphragms from ascites or pleural effusion
Usually normal

initial.why: Thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and anemia are common and often the first clue
Assesses renal function, electrolytes, and hyponatremia
Albumin, bilirubin, and aminotransferases establish synthetic function and the pattern of injury
INR reflects synthetic failure and is part of prognostic scoring
Confirms nodular liver, splenomegaly, ascites, and portal flow
Screens for varices at the time of diagnosis
Rules out pregnancy before imaging or procedures

confirmatory.why: Histology showing regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous septa is the reference standard when noninvasive testing is inconclusive
confirmatory.only_if: diagnosis remains uncertain after labs and imaging

supporting.why: Supports a hepatobiliary source when alkaline phosphatase is elevated
May support hepatic encephalopathy when the clinical picture is unclear

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.why: Evaluates suspected hepatocellular carcinoma, variceal bleeding, or vascular thrombosis
supporting.only_if: focal lesion, GI bleeding, or suspected portal vein thrombosis

supporting.why: Characterizes focal lesions or biliary disease
Identifies chronic hepatitis B as the underlying cause
Identifies chronic hepatitis C as the underlying cause

supporting.only_if: cause is unclear or there is early-onset or familial disease

not_indicated.why: Not routinely needed; reserved for suspected pleural effusion or infection
No role in the evaluation of cirrhosis
Not needed unless pancreatitis is suspected
Not part of the routine cirrhosis workup
Not indicated; encephalopathy is a metabolic diagnosis and lumbar puncture is reserved for suspected CNS infection

decision_points: Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid cell count and culture is mandatory in any patient with ascites and fever, abdominal pain, or unexplained decompensation to rule out spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Screen for varices with endoscopy at diagnosis; if none are found, repeat in 2–3 years
Begin hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance with ultrasound every 6 months once cirrhosis is confirmed
Assess MELD-Na and Child-Pugh scores to guide prognosis and transplant referral
Avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxins; adjust medication doses for hepatic impairment

criteria.name: Child-Pugh classification
criteria.summary: Grades severity of cirrhosis using total bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy; higher scores indicate worse prognosis and are grouped into classes A, B, and C.

criteria.name: MELD-Na score
criteria.summary: Estimates short-term mortality in chronic liver disease using bilirubin, INR, creatinine, and sodium; used to prioritize liver transplant allocation.

differential.name: Acute viral hepatitis
differential.why_considered: Jaundice, fatigue, nausea, and elevated aminotransferases can mimic decompensated cirrhosis
differential.trigger: Acute onset of jaundice with markedly elevated aminotransferases and no prior liver disease

history: Recent onset over days to weeks rather than years
Prodromal fever, malaise, and anorexia
Possible recent exposure or travel
exam: Tender hepatomegaly without firm nodular edge
No ascites, splenomegaly, or spider angiomata
labs: ALT often greater than 1000 U/L with ALT greater than AST
Positive hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen with IgM core antibody, or hepatitis C RNA
Normal or near-normal platelet count and INR
imaging: Ultrasound shows normal or enlarged echogenic liver without nodular contour
No splenomegaly, ascites, or portosystemic collaterals

differential.name: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
differential.why_considered: Often asymptomatic with mildly abnormal liver tests and can progress to cirrhosis, making the two difficult to separate without staging

history: Obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, or metabolic syndrome
No significant alcohol use
Usually asymptomatic or only mild fatigue
exam: May have hepatomegaly but no firm nodular edge
No spider angiomata or palmar erythema
labs: Mildly elevated ALT and AST, often ALT greater than AST
imaging: Hepatic steatosis on ultrasound without nodular contour or surface irregularity
No splenomegaly, ascites, or varices
Transient elastography shows low to intermediate stiffness

differential.name: Congestive heart failure
differential.why_considered: Leg edema, abdominal swelling, and shortness of breath overlap with cirrhotic ascites and edema
differential.trigger: Elevated jugular venous pressure with crackles and orthopnea in a patient with ascites and edema

history: Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Known coronary disease, hypertension, or valvular disease
No heavy alcohol use or viral hepatitis
exam: Elevated jugular venous pressure with prominent v waves
Ascites less prominent than peripheral edema; no spider angiomata
labs: Normal platelet count, INR, and albumin
Mild transaminase elevation from hepatic congestion
imaging: Cardiomegaly and pulmonary venous congestion on chest x-ray
Echocardiogram shows reduced ejection fraction or diastolic dysfunction
Ultrasound shows dilated hepatic veins and IVC without nodular liver

differential.name: Nephrotic syndrome
differential.why_considered: Generalized edema, ascites, and hypoalbuminemia can resemble cirrhosis

history: Periorbital edema and frothy urine
Recent infection or known glomerular disease
No alcohol use or viral hepatitis
exam: No jaundice, spider angiomata, or caput medusae
labs: Urine protein greater than 3.5 g/day with low serum albumin
Normal bilirubin, INR, and platelet count
imaging: Renal ultrasound may show normal or enlarged kidneys
Liver ultrasound is normal without nodular contour or portal hypertension

differential.name: Hepatocellular carcinoma
differential.why_considered: Can arise in cirrhosis and cause decompensation, weight loss, and abdominal pain
differential.trigger: New focal liver lesion, worsening liver function, or rising alpha-fetoprotein in a patient with cirrhosis

history: Known cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B or C
Unexplained weight loss and right upper quadrant pain
Rapid clinical deterioration
exam: Palpable hard liver nodule or mass
Signs of decompensation such as ascites or jaundice
labs: Worsening liver function tests and INR
imaging: Arterial-phase enhancing lesion with washout on multiphasic CT or MRI
Focal lesion with capsule or mosaic appearance
Portal vein invasion or thrombosis

differential.name: Primary biliary cholangitis
differential.why_considered: Chronic cholestatic liver disease that can progress to cirrhosis with jaundice and pruritus

history: Middle-aged woman with fatigue and severe pruritus
Dry eyes and dry mouth (sicca symptoms)
Gradual onset over months to years
exam: Hepatomegaly without nodular edge early on
labs: Markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT
imaging: Ultrasound shows normal biliary tree without dilation
MRCP shows normal ducts, ruling out obstruction

differential.name: Primary sclerosing cholangitis
differential.why_considered: Cholestatic liver disease that can lead to cirrhosis and portal hypertension

history: Young to middle-aged man with inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis
Fatigue, pruritus, and recurrent cholangitis
Progressive jaundice
exam: Signs of chronic liver disease may be present
imaging: MRCP shows multifocal strictures and dilatations (beaded appearance) of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts
Ultrasound may show biliary dilation or gallstones

differential.name: Hemochromatosis
differential.why_considered: Hereditary iron overload can cause cirrhosis, skin bronzing, and diabetes

history: Family history of hemochromatosis or liver disease
Arthralgia, fatigue, and erectile dysfunction
Diabetes and skin darkening
exam: Arthropathy of the hands, especially the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints
imaging: MRI shows decreased liver signal intensity on T2-weighted images due to iron deposition
Liver biopsy shows iron overload with fibrosis

differential.name: Wilson disease
differential.why_considered: Inherited copper overload can present with cirrhosis, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and hemolysis, especially in younger patients
differential.trigger: Cirrhosis in a patient under 40 with neuropsychiatric symptoms, hemolytic anemia, or Kayser-Fleischer rings

history: Young age at presentation, usually under 40
Tremor, dysarthria, or psychiatric symptoms
Family history of liver or neurologic disease
labs: Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with low haptoglobin
imaging: MRI brain shows basal ganglia signal changes
Liver biopsy shows copper accumulation and fibrosis

severity.mild: Compensated cirrhosis: no ascites, variceal bleeding, or encephalopathy; may be asymptomatic or have only fatigue and mild lab abnormalities
severity.moderate: Compensated cirrhosis with portal hypertension: thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, or small varices but no prior decompensation
severity.severe: Decompensated cirrhosis: ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, or jaundice; requires active management and transplant evaluation
severity.critical: Life-threatening decompensation: variceal hemorrhage with shock, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with sepsis, hepatorenal syndrome, or severe encephalopathy

red_flags.meaning: Variceal bleeding until proven otherwise; requires urgent endoscopy and resuscitation

red_flags.finding: Fever and abdominal pain with ascites
red_flags.meaning: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory
Hepatic encephalopathy; assess for precipitants such as infection, bleeding, or dehydration

red_flags.finding: Rapidly worsening jaundice, INR, or creatinine
red_flags.meaning: Acute decompensation or acute-on-chronic liver failure; consider urgent transplant referral
Sepsis or hemorrhage; immediate resuscitation and evaluation

complications.name: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
clues: Ascitic fluid neutrophil count greater than 250 cells/mm3

complications.name: Esophageal variceal bleeding
clues: Known varices or signs of portal hypertension

complications.name: Hepatic encephalopathy
clues: Precipitated by infection, GI bleeding, constipation, or dehydration

complications.name: Hepatorenal syndrome
clues: Absence of other causes of renal failure

complications.name: Hepatocellular carcinoma
clues: New focal liver lesion on imaging
Unexplained weight loss or right upper quadrant pain

complications.name: Coagulopathy and bleeding
clues: Easy bruising, epistaxis, or bleeding gums

complications.name: Portal vein thrombosis
clues: Sudden worsening ascites or abdominal pain
Imaging showing filling defect in portal vein

special_populations.differences: May present with confusion, falls, or failure to thrive rather than classic stigmata; symptoms are often attributed to aging. Medication sensitivity is increased due to reduced hepatic metabolism.

Can be masked by normal pregnancy changes; may present with severe pruritus, jaundice, or liver test abnormalities overlapping with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy or HELLP syndrome. Variceal bleeding risk increases with pregnancy.

Often asymptomatic and detected on routine labs; may present with unexplained hypoglycemia or worsening glycemic control due to impaired hepatic glucose handling. Metformin should be avoided in severe hepatic impairment.

Abdominal swelling may be attributed to central adiposity, delaying recognition of ascites; metabolic steatotic liver disease is the likely underlying cause. Weight loss and metabolic risk factor management are key.
Creatinine may underestimate renal impairment due to reduced muscle mass; avoid nephrotoxins and adjust medication doses. Hepatorenal syndrome is a feared complication.

Already known liver disease may present with decompensation such as encephalopathy, bleeding, or infection rather than new symptoms of cirrhosis itself. Medication dosing must be adjusted for hepatic impairment.

key_questions.question: How much alcohol have you drunk over your lifetime, and for how many years?
key_questions.looking_for: Long-standing heavy use; a strong risk factor and a treatable cause

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told you have hepatitis B or C, or had a blood transfusion or injection drug use?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic viral hepatitis or bloodborne exposure as the underlying cause

key_questions.question: When did you first notice your belly getting bigger or your legs swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Insidious onset over weeks to months; recent onset suggests decompensation

key_questions.question: Have you vomited blood or had black, tarry stools?
key_questions.looking_for: Variceal bleeding; requires urgent resuscitation and endoscopy

key_questions.question: Have you or others noticed confusion, forgetfulness, or trouble staying awake?
key_questions.looking_for: Hepatic encephalopathy; often precipitated by infection, bleeding, or dehydration

key_questions.question: Do you bruise or bleed easily, or get nosebleeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia from synthetic failure and hypersplenism

key_questions.question: Do you have any itching, yellowing of the eyes or skin, or dark urine?
Have you had fevers or new abdominal pain since your belly started swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory

key_questions.question: What medications, including acetaminophen, herbal products, or supplements, do you take?
key_questions.looking_for: Hepatotoxic exposures and drugs needing dose adjustment in hepatic impairment

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had liver disease, cirrhosis, or liver failure?
key_questions.looking_for: Hereditary hemochromatosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, or autoimmune hepatitis

key_questions.question: Have you noticed decreased sex drive, erectile problems, or breast enlargement?
key_questions.looking_for: Endocrine changes from altered hepatic hormone metabolism

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, high cholesterol, or carry extra weight around your middle?
key_questions.looking_for: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease as the underlying cause

reasoning_points: Chronic risk factor such as heavy alcohol use, viral hepatitis, or metabolic liver disease
Insidious onset of fatigue, anorexia, and weight loss over months to years
Signs of portal hypertension: ascites, splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, or varices
Signs of hepatic synthetic failure: jaundice, low albumin, elevated INR, and easy bruising
Exam stigmata such as spider angiomata, palmar erythema, or caput medusae
Complications considered and addressed: encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatorenal syndrome
Labs showing thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and coagulopathy
Imaging showing a nodular liver, splenomegaly, ascites, or portosystemic collaterals
Alternative causes excluded, including acute viral hepatitis, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, and hepatocellular carcinoma
Severity staged with Child-Pugh or MELD-Na and transplant evaluation considered when decompensated

easy: Middle-aged patient with years of heavy alcohol use
Classic stigmata: jaundice, spider angiomata, ascites, and palmar erythema
Thrombocytopenia with low albumin and elevated INR
Ultrasound shows a nodular liver with splenomegaly and ascites
medium: Patient with obesity and type 2 diabetes found to have abnormal liver tests and no alcohol history
Compensated cirrhosis detected only by thrombocytopenia and mild transaminase elevation
Ascites attributed to central adiposity, delaying recognition
Older adult presenting with confusion or falls rather than abdominal swelling
hard: Cirrhosis masked by coexisting heart failure with edema and elevated jugular venous pressure
Young patient with neuropsychiatric symptoms and hemolysis suggesting Wilson disease
Patient presenting first with variceal bleeding or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis before cirrhosis is known
Pregnant patient with pruritus and jaundice overlapping with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
New focal liver lesion with rising alpha-fetoprotein suggesting hepatocellular carcinoma
